Hello. Today's topic is ELEFAN.
ELEFAN is a method for estimating how fast fish grow, using only their lengths, even when their ages are unknown.
We will go through how it works, how to use it, and its pitfalls.
Stock assessment needs information on growth: how fast fish grow.
Usually, we read age from the rings in otoliths. But in tropical fishes, and in invertebrates such as shrimps and clams, the rings are often unclear.
Lengths, on the other hand, can be measured at markets and landing sites, cheaply, in large numbers, every month.
So, in 1981, Pauly and David developed ELEFAN. The name stands for Electronic Length Frequency Analysis.
It is still widely used in stock assessments in Southeast Asia and Africa.
The idea behind ELEFAN is very simple.
Fish born in the same year are called a cohort. Their lengths are similar, so together they form one peak in the length distribution.

This figure shows six samples, taken every two months, side by side. The vertical axis is length, and the length of each bar is the number of fish. From left to right, the peaks move up, toward larger lengths. That is growth.
Linking the peaks gives the orange dotted line. This line is the growth curve.
ELEFAN uses a computer to find the growth curve that best links the peaks.
The shape of the line is set by the von Bertalanffy growth function.
We estimate three parameters. L-infinity is the asymptotic length, the size the fish approach but do not exceed. K is the growth coefficient, the speed of growth.
t-anchor replaces t-zero from the textbook. It is the time when length is zero, in other words, the timing of recruitment, as a fraction of the year. Zero point two five means the first of April.
For fish whose growth changes with the seasons, two more parameters, C and t-s, can be added.
Now for the three steps. Step one is restructuring.
The top panel shows one month's length frequencies. The black line is a moving average, here over five length classes.

In the bottom panel, each class count is divided by the moving average, and one is subtracted. Classes above the moving average become positive peaks, shown in orange. Classes below become negative troughs, shown in blue.
Look at the small orange bars on the left. Where counts are low, random bumps also become peaks. This is the root of a pitfall we will see later.
Step two is scoring.
Choose one growth curve and apply it to every year's cohort, and you get several lines like these.
Add up the values where the lines pass. Peaks count as plus, troughs as minus. This sum is called E S P. The sum of all available peaks, the maximum possible score, is called A S P.
Dividing E S P by A S P, and transforming the result, gives the score, R-n. The higher R-n is, the better the curves follow the peaks.
Step three is to search for the combination of L-infinity, K and t-anchor with the highest score.

This figure shows how the score changes as one parameter changes. There is one large peak, but the line is jagged, with many small peaks. A simple hill-climbing method gets stuck on a small peak, like the open circle.

Next, four pitfalls to watch for.
First, settings change the answer. Changing the width of the moving average, or of the length classes, moves the estimates.
Second, the seesaw between L-infinity and K. A large L-infinity with a small K, and the reverse, can fit about equally well.
Third, fish of the same age still differ in length. When this variation is large, the cohort peaks blur, and K is easily misestimated.

Fourth, even pure noise, data with no growth information at all, will give a plausible K, because ELEFAN picks up chance peaks. Getting an answer is not evidence that the data contain growth information.
This is the most important message today.
ELEFAN always returns an answer, whatever the data. A high score does not mean the growth estimate is right.
Treat the ELEFAN result as a hypothesis, and check it before you use it.
So how can we check it? Let's go down the table.
First, fix L-infinity from other information, such as the maximum length. This stops the seesaw, so ELEFAN only needs to estimate K.
Second, sample hundreds of fish every month, for at least a year. Tracking peaks needs both many samples and many fish.
Third, compare the results across different moving-average widths and class widths. If the settings move the answer, the answer is weak.
Fourth, use a bootstrap to get a range of estimates. The R package fishboot can do this.
Fifth, check against other methods, such as otoliths or tagging.

Finally, errors in K carry over into mortality. The slope of a length-converted catch curve is Z over K, so if K is a third of its true value, so is Z. The stock would look healthier than it really is.
To sum up.
First, ELEFAN finds growth curves from the movement of peaks in length data.
Second, it splits the data into peaks and troughs, and picks the curve that best follows the peaks: the one with the highest score, R-n.
Third, the answer is a hypothesis. Watch out for settings, individual variation and noise, and check it before you use it.
